about: The words of the cards of Data/encounters/england_south_east_793.json (the region england_south_east: Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic, Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Dommoc), with a picture line for each card (art.<card id>) and the news items the cards post. Written 7 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Riddles said aloud are our own plain renderings of the Exeter Book's (Tupper 1910 for the text) and of Aldhelm's and Tatwine's; nothing is quoted from a modern translation. People say days by feasts and moons.

entries.text: Wine over the side
A Frankish hull rides off the hard on the last of the flood, not let land. Her master has brought his boat alongside yours, on the side away from the hall, and keeps his voice down.

Evening at high water off a gravel beach: a small Frisian boat afloat with a deeper ship's boat hard against her far side, two men passing a cask across the gunwales, thatched roofs and a long hall on the bluff behind, the light going.
Six tides I have lain here looking at your beach. The reeve says my king's ports are shut to his king's people, so his are shut to me. My wine does not know this.
Two casks of Rhine wine, thirty-five pennies each. On your Strand tomorrow they are worth twice that, with a Frisian's name on them.
The reeve's king cut off a king's head this year, I hear. I do not blame the reeve for keeping his own on.
The last time we dealt, somebody on the bank was counting. It cost you, I am told. So today I ask less, and we go round the far side of her.
You bought from me before and nobody the wiser. I told my steersman: that is a Frisian who looks at the bank first.
Buy his two casks over the side, with nobody to witness (70 d)
Tell him of a beach to the west, where another king's reeve looks at the sky
Say you buy before witnesses or not at all
Water made bone
In the king's hall the reeve has finished with the morning's sales. He pushes the tally sticks to one side, looks at you as he did the first day, and says he has a question that is not about cargo.

A dim timber hall smelling of rushes and smoke: a grey-fair reeve in a green cloak behind a table of tally sticks laid out by length, one hand flat on a wax tablet, a Frisian master standing before him cap in hand, two spearmen on the bench by the door.
They say the reeve at the Stour landing passes a ship free for a riddle answered to his face. I will not be outdone by a Kentish landing.
I saw a thing go on its way, wonderfully decked. A wonder on the wave: water turned to bone. Say what I saw. I shall say it once more, and then you may go.
You took it away with you. Has the answer changed on the water? Mine has not.
No head for riddles, you said. A man who can reckon a toll in his head has head enough. Try again.
You have the look of a man carrying something up the hill. Put it on the table. Then put it there again.
Your keel has no notch on my stick. I cut none, and I remember why. Ask me a thing twice some day; I should like to see how it feels.
The potter's forty crates. He paid a man with a rod and no knife? That would be my sister's son. He is no longer my man. Tell the potter the stick is cut.
The old king is dead and the riddle is the same. That is more than can be said of most things in this hall.
Take the riddle away with you
Give him the answer, twice, the same both times
Ask about the Gipeswic potter's forty crates
Say you have no head for riddles, and ask about the tide
Vouched at the king's hall

A Kentish man has come up from the hard with two pairs of black stones on a barrow and you beside them. Another man has laid his hand on the stones and says they were stolen from him. By the law of his own kings the Kentishman names the one who sold them, at the king's hall in the wic.

The porch of a long timber hall: a reeve with a rod of office, a countryman with one hand on a barrow of grey quernstones, a Frisian merchant between them, a tonsured priest waiting to one side with a small book, townspeople looking on from the road.
I bought these stones from this Frisian at the last spring tide, on the open hard. Now a Rochester man says they are his. I name the Frisian. Let him answer for them.
The law is old and plain. He names you. You show where the stones came from, or swear at the altar they were yours to sell. Or give him his price back.
I counted what came off your keel that tide. I can say so, if I am asked. I am waiting to be asked.
And there is the matter of a sale over a gunwale that nobody witnessed. It makes a hall think.
If it comes to the altar, bring one who saw you land them. An oath is not lighter for being said quickly.
Ask the reeve to say what he counted off your keel
Walk up to Saint Paul's and swear at the altar that they were yours to sell
Give the buyer his price back and take the stones (24 d)
Ask the hall for a day, till the next moot
The moneyer's pan
At the moneyers' benches the hammer stops. Ibba wipes his hands on his scorched apron, looks at your purse, and then reaches under the counter for something wrapped in a rag.

An open-fronted shed with a locked door: a thick-armed moneyer in a scorched leather apron holding a small gold coin up between finger and thumb to a merchant, a balance and a touchstone on the counter, a second man astride a die block behind with his hammer lowered.
Deniers? In the pan. You get the king's new pennies for the weight, less my cut, less the fire. Before that, look at this. Look, do not touch.
Your silver was good last time. So I shall show you the thing again, and you will tell me again that you do not know.
The king's name in the middle, and round it marks no priest can read. A pilgrim brought the pattern home in his shoe. I cut what I saw, not what I understood.
Saracens' writing, you said. Their king's year and their god's name, and ours set in the middle upside down. I have thought of little else. I have not told the reeve.
The penny is heavier this year, by the king's order, so you get fewer. Sigh at the king. He is not here, which is why people sigh at me.
A Frisian with rings on his fingers once brought me a bag of bad deniers and smiled. If you know him, tell him the pot is still hot.
What have you there? A little pan on a chain, and emperors rubbed flat. Lay them on the counter. No, in a row. I want to see who they agree with.
Tell him whose writing it is: you have held such a coin
Leave the old weights with him for an afternoon, and be taught them
Have your purse weighed, and say you do not know the marks
Ground on a dish
On the road up from the shore a baker stands in his doorway holding the top stone of a quern, worn so thin that the light comes through the eye. He has heard a Frisian keel is in.

A metalled road between thatched houses end-on to the street: a floury man in a doorway holding up a thin grey quernstone so the daylight shows through its hole, loaves on a board beside him, a pig rooting in the road.
Look at that. Nine winters of barley. You can read through her. Every house on this road is grinding on a dish, and the reeve turns the stone ships away.
When the kings have done sulking, the first man to land black stones here names his price. I will take eight pairs for the street, of the old thickness.
They say the kings have made it up, and the stones may come. Then where are they? I have flour to make and a dish to make it on.
You have stones in her now? Do not take them down to the hard. Bring them to my door.
You took my order. I have told the street. Do not make a liar of me in front of bakers.
Take his order: eight pairs of black stones, of the old thickness
Sell him four pairs at his door (80 d)
Say you carry wine this voyage, and go on up the road
Leofrun's looms
Two looms thump against the back wall and a girl is counting clay rings aloud. Leofrun measures you with her eye, as she would a length of cloth, and goes on working.

Inside a wide thatched house: two upright looms hung with rows of clay rings, a lean woman in a linen cap holding a brown cloak up against a merchant to measure it, folded cloaks on a chest, a girl counting weights, a dye vat steaming in the yard beyond.
Looking or buying? Looking is free until you touch. That one is sold. That one is sold. That one you cannot afford.
The Frisian. Mind the weights. I have six finished and two on the loom, and I know what you gave last time.
The Franks say our cloaks are short. They buy by the piece and want them by the ell. So would I. But why do they want them longer? Nobody has told me.
So two kings have written to each other about my work. The old length, they say. Then the old price. I have told the reeve so.
A count at Dorestat wants one of the old length? His steward ordered one once and has not paid. This time half goes on the chest before the shuttle moves.
From Hildgyth? Then you have been to Dofras. She asks why the Franks want them longer. Tell her I asked first.
You paid the second half on the day. I have told the wool man. He did not believe a Frisian would.
Order six cloaks and pay half beforehand (45 d)
Buy a short one off the chest (16 d)
Give her Hildgyth's question from Dofras
Look, touch nothing, and go
Off the loom
Six cloaks lie folded on the chest, brown and grey and one dyed with madder. Leofrun runs her thumb down a selvedge and waits to be paid the other half.

A chest in a weaver's house with six folded cloaks on it, one red among brown and grey, a woman's hand resting on the pile, a bone weaving sword stuck in her belt, the looms behind already warped for the next.
Six, as ordered. Count the picks if you like; I did. The other half on the chest, and then they are yours and the weather's.
The long one is on top. It took the wool of a cloak and a third. If your count stands up in it and it is short, the fault is in the count.
Keep them dry and folded, not rolled. And if a Frank asks who wove them, say a woman who expects to be paid.
You left them on my chest a fortnight more. I sold none of them. I thought about it.
Pay the other half and take the six (45 d)
Pay, and have the long one wrapped apart for the count (45 d)
Ask her to keep them till the next spring tide
The comb-maker's yard
The yard is white with the dust of antler and bone. Hunfrith sits astride his bench sawing teeth into a plate, coughs, loses count, and starts the comb again.

A small yard behind a house, white underfoot: a thin dusty man on a low bench sawing teeth into an antler plate clamped between his knees, finished combs on a string by the door, a pit of sawn tines in the corner, a bundle of notched tally sticks spilled on the ground.
Combs? A man who buys one comb has lice. A man who buys a hundred has a ship. Which are you?
I owe you or you owe me. My sister will know. Sit there. Not there, that is the saw.
Bring me antler. Red deer, shed or cut, I am not proud. A Northman showed me one as long as my arm and flat like a hand. I dream about it.
Is that antler in your boat? Do not show it to anybody else. Do not show it to my sister either; she will want to know what I paid.
I have twelve tallies and I cannot say which are debts and which are sales. If Leofrun reads them before I do, I am a dead man with clean hair.
You sorted my sticks. I have kept them sorted. Nearly.
Take his order for antler: six bundles, at a comb-maker's price
Sell him the antler you carry (2 bundles, 20 d)
Buy three dozen combs at the bench (27 d)
Sort his tally sticks for him before his sister comes
Three nights

Tatberht's yard, by the west road: a long house with a loft, a barred store, a well lined with an old wine cask, a dog that knows who has paid. The host is whittling a sheep's bone on the step and counting his guests on his fingers.

A fenced yard at dusk seen from its gate: a broad stooped man whittling a bone on the step of a long thatched house, a wiry old pilot with a sounding pole asleep against the loft ladder, a cask-lined well, a broken Roman wall and a church on a hill beyond the fence.
Dorestat? Then you sleep here. One night you are a guest, three nights you are my trouble. Leave your knife on the peg.
Your bed is where it was. Nobody has died in it since. Sit, eat, and tell me who is on the water.
Two Frisians, a Dane buying hones who asks about the river, and a man with rings on his fingers in the best bed. He asked your name. He asks everybody's.
She shoals off the Fleet mouth since the winter. Take the flood at its second hour, north side. I could show you the whole river from the Nore, if the nights were long enough.
The nights are long enough now. Thirty pennies and my ale, and by Candlemas you will know the sands as I do. Better: your eyes are younger.
This? My name. Tatberht. That stave is the T. A Frisian of this yard taught my grandfather, or so we tell guests.
You paid for three nights and gave no trouble. I told the reeve so. He asked me twice.
Lodge the crew three nights (4 d)
Winter here and learn the Thames marks from the old pilot (30 d)
Tell him who is on the water, and hear who asked after you
Sleep aboard and save the pennies
The notched stick

Wynflaed's alehouse: a bush on a pole, a notched stick over the lintel for every crew that owes, four tongues at once. She points into a corner with her ladle, where a young man is making one cup last the evening.

A low smoky alehouse with benches along both walls and a fire in the middle of the floor: a sturdy woman in a striped apron pointing an iron ladle at a young sailor hunched over a cup in the corner, a notched stick hanging above the door, dice on a board.
A new face. Sit where I can see your hands. News is free if you bring some.
You. You paid last time; I looked at the stick. Your corner is free and the eel is fresh if you are quick.
That one in the corner. His ship floated off without him. He rows, he does not steal, and he owes me eight pennies. Hire him and pay me.
I pull a good oar and I can splice. I was asleep in the wrong house when the tide served. It will not happen twice.
The reeve's men drank quiet last night. When they drink quiet, somebody is turned away at the next tide. Is your master a Frank? No. Then drink.
A crew in from the north coast would not say what they saw. Then they drank, and said. Go and ask the priest about buckets.
A Thanet ship called the Sheldrake? Nine summers back a corn factor waited a week on the hard for her and drank on the stick. Ask at the breaking beach. Old hulls end there.
The hand you took off my stick. Does he still row? Then I did you both a kindness, and you may pay for this cup.
Clear his eight pennies and take him aboard
Buy the crew a round and listen (3 d)
Tell her you have hands enough
The breaking beach

At the upstream end of the hard a big clinker ship lies on her side, half stripped, her clench bolts dropping one by one into a basket. The wright sights along a new keel with one eye shut, and does not look round.

The upstream end of a gravel hard: a large clinker hull on her side with half her strakes off, a basket of iron bolts beneath, a wright sighting along a new keel on blocks, heaps of Roman tile and oak chips, tar smoke blowing over the river.
She was a good ship. Now she is good iron and bad firewood. Every bolt in that basket was drawn straight. A boy sells the bent ones for bread.
Is that tar I smell on you, or only a Frisian? If it is tar, name a price before the Kentish men hear.
A Kentish man found her on the sands in the river mouth, nine summers back. Mast gone, nobody aboard, corn sprouting in her bilge. Her stem is yonder: a duck's head.
You took the duck's head. Somebody on Thanet will know it. I would not want to be the one who carries it there. I am glad it is you.
The new one is for a man of this town. Oak from up the river, felled at the right moon. Do not lean on her.
Buy a keg of drawn bolts and roves (10 d)
Sell him a barrel of tar (28 d)
Ask for the carved stem-piece, for a woman at Sarre
Watch a strake come off, and go
The pens by the north ditch

Hurdle pens on trampled ground at the town's edge: red cattle, sheep, pigs under an oak. A herdsman leans on a hurdle with two long-legged hounds lying at his feet, and Cynred the wool man is feeling a fleece as if it owed him money.

Hurdle pens on trampled ground with open pasture beyond a ditch: a herdsman leaning on a pen with two lean long-legged hounds at his feet, a round-faced man in a sheepskin jerkin feeling a fleece, tally sticks at his belt, butchers at a bench by the ditch.
Wool or hides? Feel that. That is from above Dorchester, the long kind. I can let you have it on the tally, if the reeve knows you.
You again. Sit; there is new fleece in from the valley, and I have a thing to ask you.
A bitch and a young dog, one litter. They go together or they stay. Seventy pennies the pair, before the reeve's man, and I will not be hurried.
For a count over the sea? Then he will hang whoever parts them. Good. Tell him so from me.
A wool man at Hamwic owes me for half a thin year's fleece. His port is open, he says. Then he can pay. Take him my half of the stick; a bale is yours.
You have been to Hamwic. I can tell by your face that he paid something. Count it out where the herdsman can see.
I have wool in a sealed ship on the Canche. Every wet day I feel it in my teeth.
You brought Leofstan's silver back counted. I burned my half of the stick. There is always a bale put by for you.
Buy the pair before the reeve's man (72 d)
Take Cynred's half of the tally to Hamwic
Count out Leofstan's thirty pennies to Cynred
Feel the fleece, say it is good, and go on
A grave on the western rise

A Frisian steersman of another Dorestat boat died in Tatberht's loft on his third night, of a fever. This morning he is carried up to the graves on the western rise, among the thorn trees. His own ship floated off on the dawn tide; she had a wind.

A windy rise above gravel pits with graves among thorn trees: a tall tonsured priest with a small book at the head of an open grave, a stooped host with a ring of keys, four men lowering a body sewn in sailcloth, the river bright below.
Three nights under my roof, so I answer for him, and I bury him. His master left four pennies and his sea chest, and went out on the tide. A wind does not wait.
Nobody here knows his name. His master called him Steersman. I shall bury him as God's servant from Dorestat, and God will know which. Stand at the foot; he should have a countryman.
A candle at the head costs what wax costs. He has four pennies to his name, and they are the gravedigger's.
There is the chest. A knife, a comb, a lump of amber, a child's shoe. Somebody at Dorestat is waiting for a man and will get a box. Better from a Frisian's hand.
You paid for a stranger's candle on this rise once. I have not forgotten whose it was.
Pay for the wax and the Mass (6 d)
Take his sea chest home to Dorestat
Stand at the foot of the grave till it is filled
The priest of Saint Paul's

A short walk east, over the Fleet and in by a gate with no doors, the bishop's church stands among brambles and fallen walls. A tall priest with ink on two fingers comes out to see who has walked so far from the beach.

A timber church on a hill among Roman ruins and brambles: a tall tonsured priest with a leather satchel at the door, a small wheeled chair standing by a shrine inside, men with a cart pulling down a ruin for its stone, rooks in a broken tower.
God be with you. You have come from over the water. Have you any books aboard? No. Nobody has. Come in out of the wind.
The merchant who listens. Good. I have a letter for the Kentish shore and nobody honest to carry it. You see where this is going.
It is Saint Alban's eve, did you know? No. He died a day's ride north of here, for a priest he had hidden. We keep his day tomorrow.
The heathen have burnt Saint Cuthbert's church in the north. Master Alcuin has written of it. I read the letter twice, and then I went and counted our buckets.
It is a fast today, so I cannot offer you meat, and on other days I cannot afford to. Sit anyway.
The archbishop is out of Kent, and his books went another way. Did they get over the water? Say only yes or no. I shall write it small.
They say the East Angles' new bishop wants Bede copied. We have no Bede either. If it is to be written once, it could be written twice.
You took my letter to the Kentish shore. Did the scribe read it standing up? He does that when it is bad news.
Ask for a copy of Alcuin's letter, to be read aboard (4 d for the skin)
Carry his letter to the scribes of Christ Church
Sell him the book you carry, for the bishop's church (380 d)
Hear the office, and walk back before the tide
Oak from the Lea

The hithe under the old wall is heaped with ship's timber: strakes, knees, whole stems with beasts' heads on them. The men of London have fetched the Danes' ships down from the Lea. What they could not bring away they broke up.

A timber river front under an old stone wall heaped with broken ship timbers and carved beast-headed stems, a lean reeve with a knotted measuring cord and a wax tablet standing among them, small boats towing a dismasted longship downriver behind.
The king had the river staked above them, so they left their ships and went overland. We fetched what was worth fetching. The rest is on this shore, by the ealdorman's leave.
Good oak, Danish-built and dry. I am selling it by the load before the bishops' men ask for it as a gift. Three loads to a keel your size, no more.
A Frisian will know what oak is worth where there are no trees. I do not ask. I only take the king's part of the sale.
Buy three loads of the Danes' oak (54 d)
Buy one load (18 d)
Look over the beast-heads, and buy nothing
The beast that looks back

On the south side of Saint Paul's churchyard a slab stands on edge, painted dark blue, red and white: a great beast looking back over its own shoulder, tangled with a snake, and a line of runes along the rim. An old housecarl stands before it with his hat in his hand.

A churchyard under lime trees: a stone slab set on edge and painted dark blue, red and white with a backward-looking beast caught in a snake, runes cut along its rim, a grey-bearded man with a gilded axe on his shoulder standing bareheaded before it.
Ginna and Toki had this stone laid. It says so, there, along the edge. It does not say for whom. I know for whom. I rowed beside him.
We fought against this town more than once and it stood. Now we lie in its churchyard under our own letters. The priest allows the beast because of the cross on the other side.
You have a little of our tongue. Then hear what we said over him, the old words. The priest need not know.
You have not our tongue. A pity. There are words for a grave that do not go into English.
You heard the old words here once. Say them over me, if you are in the town when it is time.
Hear the old words said at the grave
Ask him to show you which stave is which
Leave a penny for the priest's box
The double tide

A short thick man with an eel spear over his shoulder and a sounding pole taller than himself wades out to look at how your boat sits on the gravel. He looks at the boat a good deal longer than he looks at you.

A long shelving beach of gravel and grey mud with clinker hulls drawn up stern to the water: a short weathered man, bare legs grey with mud, leaning on a tall sounding pole beside a small Frisian boat, flat wide light off the water behind.
You came up well. Most strangers wait for the ebb and get half of one. She floods twice here. Did nobody tell you?
I saw your sail at the spit and said to the reeve: the small Frisian. He said: good, he pays.
Soft mud both sides, all the way down. You can sit a boat on it and take no hurt. Getting her off is another prayer.
My brother rode down to Portland strand behind the reeve, to greet three ships. So now I look at how a ship sits before I wave.
You have the long song? From the old man at Dofras, I suppose. He ends it wrong. Sit; I will give you the true ending while the tide stands.
You know the water now as well as a stranger can. Keep the dead tree on the oak wood. And do not tell the Frisian with the cord what I showed you.
I took you down last time and you touched nothing. You listen. That is rarer than a fair wind.
Hire him down the long water on the next stand (3 d)
Walk the shore with him at low water and learn the creeks (20 d)
Buy a barrel of his eels (8 d)
Thank him, and say you will find your own way down
A fare for the Seine
On the hythe the priest of the shore church stands beside a man with a staff and a wallet, and looks along the row of hulls for one that is bound south. He has seen yours.

A gravel beach with boats drawn up: a thin stooped priest with a wax tablet at his girdle and a broad countryman with a staff and a wallet, both looking at a small Frisian boat being loaded, porters wading past with casks.
This man goes to the thresholds of the Apostles, and he is what he says. I have looked in his wallet: bread, a spare shoe, and a tablet for a canon at Rouen.
A ship-master took the holy Willibald over from this water for a fare, in my grandfather's day. They pitched their tents by the river at Rouen. The fare has gone up.
I can pay six pennies, or I can pull an oar and pray. I am better at the second. I have never been in a boat.
The Franks' king lets true pilgrims land though his ports are shut to our traders. This one carries no bundle. I am tired of blessing bundles.
You took my last pilgrim over for nothing. He sent word from Rouen: he was sick the whole way and has never been so well treated.
Take him for his prayers, and the priest's tablet with him
Take him to Rouen for his six pennies
Say you are not bound for the Seine
The reeve's table

It is a feast day, and the king's reeve keeps open board in the king's yard for the masters who feed his beach. Meat is roasting. Herewald sits at the head with a small bronze spoon that has two prongs at its other end, and uses it for oysters.

A fenced yard with a long thatched house and a carved door-frame: a broad red-faced man at the head of a trestle table lifting an oyster with a small bronze spoon, ship-masters of several peoples on the benches, meat on a spit, two horses under a lean-to.
A Frisian. Good. Sit below the Frank and above the Kentishman; that is how the beach stands this year. You sell before witnesses here, and I am usually one of them.
Your boat I know by her patch. Sit where you sat. The king's share is the same, and so am I.
A king's order about Frankish ships? I have not seen it. If I see it I must obey it, so I take care where I look.
Our lady the queen is King Offa's daughter. So we love the Mercians here. Say that I said so, if anybody on the Strand asks you.
The wic-reeve at Lundenwic sent to ask what passes through my beach. I answered that the tide does, twice.
This? It came from the king's own board. One end for the oyster, the other for whatever is left. Nobody else in Wessex has one, and nobody else wants one.
You set wine on my table at a feast. I have not forgotten the cask, or the man.
Set a cask of your wine on his table
Ask him to witness your sales himself
Eat, listen, and say little
Count them for me

A tall old man in a mail shirt and a dark red cloak stands in the gateway of the king's yard, with a boy behind him holding his helm. He has been asking every master on the beach the same thing, and now he asks you.

The gateway of a fenced royal yard: a tall spare old man with a white moustache in mail and a dark red cloak, a worn silver-pommelled sword at his side, a boy behind him holding a helm, a Frisian master pointing out to sea.
You are the Frisian from the beach. What sails did you see between Wight and here? Count them for me. Slowly.
The merchant who can count. Good. Stand here. Tell me again what you saw off the Franks' shore.
A day's notice turns a slaughter of townsmen into a slaughter of raiders. I have the shire, and the mud. The mud is the better soldier.
They have burned your Dorestat, and burned it again. The same keels look into every river mouth on the way home. This one has no wall, and the king has no ships.
Your count was true. I told the king whose it was.
You counted gulls for me last time. A man may be wrong. Do not be wrong again.
Tell him every sail you passed, by her cut and her course
Sell a cask of ale to the men he has called out (14 d)
Say you saw nothing but fishermen
The cask and the cup

A small timber church a little above the tide line, a wooden cross before its door. Inside it smells of beeswax and damp thatch, and the sea can be heard through the wall. The priest has a wax tablet on his knee, and looks up like a man who has been waiting for somebody to try a thing on.

Inside a small plank church: a thin tonsured priest on a bench with a wax tablet on his knee, one small window of greenish glass throwing a spot of light on the altar cloth, a merchant in the doorway with the grey sea behind him.
God keep you. You came in on the second high water, I think. Bede knew about that. Do sailors read Bede? No. Sit down.
The Frisian who listens. Good. I have a new one for you.
I am a house that holds what makes men glad. I drown nobody, though many have been lost in me. Oak made me and hoops bind me. Bishop Aldhelm said it better.
You have the cask and the cup on my tablet. The third is not in any book of mine. Ask the woman who sells ale, and then ask the one who cuts bone.
Six pilgrims went over on Thursday, each with a square bundle. Do you carry men to God or cloth to market? I ask everyone. I shall pray for you either way.
The abbot at Dommoc says I have a word of the cask wrong? Which word? No, do not tell me. I shall find it myself, and then I shall write to him.
The east window wants glass. The light comes in green through one pane and plain through the other three. I notice it at Mass, which I should not.
Four panes of one colour. I say your house's name at the altar, and the light falls on the cloth as I say it. Come and see.
Ask for the cask and the cup written on a tablet
Give a crate of glass for the east window
Hear Mass before you load, not after
A fast day
It is a fast day. The bell at Saint Mary's is struck by hand for the hours, no meat is on any fire in the town, and Beorngyth is carrying a covered pot up from the alehouse to the priest.

A wide fenced graveyard on low ground above a beach of boats: a sturdy woman in a clean linen head-cloth carrying a covered pot toward a timber church, a man striking a hand bell at its door, rooks, a grey still morning.
Eel broth for the priest. It is a fast, so he may have fish, and I may have the thanks. The eels have small bones in them. Ask for bread with yours.
No meat today in any house that wants to be buried from that church. The Frankish masters complain. Then they eat my eels and stop.
Is that herring in your boat? On a fast day? Do not take it to the strand. Bring it to my door, and then to the minster's, in that order.
Your men are looking at the smith's bacon. Feed them fish before they look harder, or the priest will hear of it from me, and I shall be sorry.
You kept the last fast with the town. It was noticed. Everything is, here.
Somebody saw smoke from your boat last fast day, and it did not smell of fish. I said it was tar. I do not say it twice.
Sell her a barrel of herring for the fast (16 d)
Keep the fast with the town: eel broth for the crew (3 d)
Let the crew eat their bacon aboard, out of sight
Four staves on a cow's toe

Three open sheds on the street down to the hythe. In the nearest a small woman saws cattle bone into plates on a block that is the grey backbone of a whale. She asks what a thing is made of before she asks what it costs.

An open-sided shed white with bone dust: a small wiry woman in a linen cap sawing a plate of bone on a grey whale-vertebra block, finished combs hanging on a string like fish, a cow's toe bone scratched with four runes on the shelf behind her.
Mind the block. It is a whale's back. No, I did not catch it. What have you got that is antler?
The Frisian with the small boat. Did you bring antler? Then sit anyway. You can hold the plate while I saw.
I cut my name on a cow's toe. Four staves. The Frisian with the cord says one is wrong. I say it is mine and I may spell it how I like.
There were mounds where the houses by the cross street stand. Spears in them, the old people said. The priest threw the bones out with the rubbish. Some were my kin.
A man on the Strand says a comb does not need to be read. His do not need to be counted either, I hear, since he cannot.
You bring antler and you hold the plate straight. Give me your hand. Four staves. I shall show you each, and which one the Frisian says is wrong.
Your house's name is on a plate of mine, four staves and a fish. If you lose that comb, do not come back and tell me.
Sell her the antler you carry (2 bundles, 18 d)
Learn her four staves
Have your house's name cut on a comb (12 d)
Hold the plate while she saws
What the Frank's king has done
In Beorngyth's alehouse a Frankish master has the bench by the door and the black jug in front of him, which means he paid first. He is telling the room what his king has done.

A long alehouse by lamplight, a bush on a pole outside the open door: a well-fed Frankish ship-master on the bench by the door with a black jug before him, one hand raised to the room, a sturdy ale-wife with wet sleeves watching him with her arms folded.
I had it at Rouen from the abbot's own toll man. The king has taken off his order. English cloth may land on the Seine again, and the first bolts in will sell dear.
I am telling you as a friend. Buy every cloak on this strand tonight and be at Rouen before the Frisians hear. I would do it myself, but I am loaded.
A Frisian on the Strand at Lundenwic told me of this beach when the reeve there turned me off. I owe your people a good turn. This is it.
A Frank sits on that bench every moon and tells me what his king will do. Ale is a penny. News like that I give away, since I get it for nothing.
The wool man will sell you cloth tonight at any price you name, and laugh till morning. He has been shut out of that fair six years. Ask him if it is open.
Buy six bolts of cloth tonight, at tonight's price (120 d)
Buy the Frank a cup and let him talk (2 d)
Ask Beorngyth how old his news is
A Frank's news
Beorngyth's alehouse, a moon later. The bench by the door has a Kentish man on it, and the black jug is back on its shelf.

The same alehouse by day, the door open on the gravel street: the bench by the door taken by a stranger, a black jug standing on a high shelf, the ale-wife leaning in the doorway with a dipper, looking amused.
The Frank who sat there went home on the next fair wind. His king's ports are as shut as they were. They turned an English keel off the Seine last week, cloth and all.
You bought cloth on his word. I did tell you. Well, cloth keeps. It keeps better than a Frank's news.
You asked me how old his news was. It was not old. It was not born. Here, the first cup is mine.
You bought him a cup. So did everybody. He drank a week on that story and never told it the same way twice.
Do you know why he said it? He had wine to sell, and a room full of men counting what they will make at Rouen buys wine. I should have charged him.
Laugh, and stand the house a round (4 d)
Sell the six bolts back at what the wool house gives (84 d)
Say nothing, and remember what a Frank's news is worth
The wool houses
A row of house-ends with plank doors and no windows. One stands open on wool sacks to the rafters. A tall fair man in a red tunic has a bolt of cloth out at arm's length, and is arguing with it.

A row of windowless house-ends on a gravel street, one door open on wool sacks piled to the rafters: a tall fair man in a madder-red tunic holding a bolt of cloth at arm's length, small shears on a thong at his neck, a dog asleep on the best cloth.
Leofstan. Wool, mostly. Feel that: she is from ewes six winters old, and no Frisian has had his thumb on her yet.
The Dorestat boat. Come in out of the wind. I have a bolt put by that I would not show your friend with the tally stick.
The fair of Saint-Denis opens on the saint's own day. A day and a night to Rouen, then the river. I have missed six. I do not mean to miss a seventh.
The ports are open and the shearing is in. I have more wool than my one ship carries. Take the rest at the shed price, and we shall talk about wine after.
There is a Leofstan at Lundenwic whose wool went sour under a Frankish seal. Not me. People pay me his sympathy and him my bills.
That is Cynred's half of the stick. So he has sent a Frisian for it. He is not angry, he says? He never is. That is what frightens me.
You took Cynred his thirty. Did he burn the stick? Then I owe him only the other thirty, and he will send you again.
Buy six sacks of the new wool at the shed price (36 d)
Buy three bolts of his cloth (42 d)
Lay Cynred's half of the tally on the trestle
Feel the fleece, and agree that she is good
Three strakes off

South of the houses the gravel gives way to salt marsh and a shingle spit. On the last firm ground a hull lies on her side with three strakes off, new oak pale against the old, and a pitch pot smokes over a fire of offcuts.

A shingle spit beside a salt marsh and a still lagoon: a clinker hull on her side with three pale new strakes among the grey, a wright with an adze, a pitch pot smoking over a small fire, wide grey water running down toward a far island.
Oak from the woods behind the water, nails from the smiths at the north crossing. I build one a winter, and mend what the mud sends me the rest of the year.
A ship my grandfather built, of oak felled the year after King Pippin died, lies on an island of the Frisians, they tell me. Is she still tight? Nobody ever comes back to say.
I have a load of planks split and no keel to put them on till the frost. A Frisian has no trees. Twenty-four pennies, and you may count the knots.
Rhine nails? Show me. Our smiths make a good nail, but they make it slowly, and they both stop when either one is thirsty.
You took my planks over the sea. Did they sell? Do not tell me for how much.
Buy his load of split oak (24 d)
Sell him a keg of ship nails (20 d)
Watch the new strake go on
Say it back to me

Townspeople are carrying what they can over the ferry to the old stone work across the river. A widow has stopped on the mud below the walls with nothing in her hands at all, which among so many bundles is what makes you look.

Grey walls of flint and red tile higher than a house on a river bank, elder growing from the top: townspeople with bundles climbing out of a flat ferry boat on the mud, one woman standing apart with empty hands, looking at a merchant.
My sons are with the shire. If the ships come I go to Winchester on my feet. What I had is in the ground behind my house, and a house can burn.
I shall tell one person who is not of this town, so it is not all in one head. You are a Frisian. Gone on the tide, and back when it is over.
From my back door post, toward the well, nine paces. Then a forearm deep, under the hearth stone I am not using. Say it back to me.
The ealdorman beat them on the beach, and then died of it. They will come again. The mud does not die, but it cannot be everywhere.
Say it back to her, twice, and keep it
Tell her it is too much to put in a stranger's head
Two sons and a spade
Grass grows in the strand street, and half the roofs are down. Two men with a spade have been asking along the shore for a Frisian their mother spoke of before she died at Winchester.

A gravel street going to grass between roofless timber houses: two countrymen with a spade standing by a burnt door post and a fallen well, four shallow holes dug behind them, a merchant pacing out a line with his arm stretched toward the well.
Our mother said: a Frisian with a small boat knows where. She would not tell us. She said two boys talk. She was right, we do.
The door post is burnt and the well is fallen in. We have dug in four places. Nine paces from where? Toward what?
We mean to build on the new ground, by the other water. There is a tenth in it for you, and a door there that is yours while there is a roof on it.
Pace it out for them: door post, well, nine, a forearm deep
Tell them it will cost half
Counted at the ford
At the town end of the ford stand a hurdle shelter, a bundle of tally sticks, and the king's reeve, whichever king that is this year, counting aloud what comes off your boat.

A gravel ford going down into a brown river at low water: a broad short man with tally sticks at his belt counting on his fingers under a hurdle shelter, a thin clerk with a wax tablet at his elbow, a Frisian keel aground behind on a bank faced with posts and hurdles.
A Dorestat boat. Good. Stand there while I count what comes off her. It is not that I doubt you. It is that I count.
I know the boat and I know the man. Tell me what is under the sailcloth and we shall both be home sooner.
The king over our king wants no Frankish hulls on English ground. He said it at Tamworth. Things said at Tamworth arrive here quite tired.
No Frankish hull may land on this bank. That is the king's word, and I say it loudly, as you hear. The Stoke bank I cannot see after dark. That I say quietly.
Whose ship, whose goods, whose man. I write all three. The reeve counts; I write. Between us nothing is missed.
Three kings since I took the sticks. The river has not asked me the name of one of them.
Black stones were sold on the Cornhill that I never counted. I cannot think how. Sit down.
The clerk was awake. I said after dark; I did not say which dark. There was nothing I could do.
Land what you carry by daylight, with the due and a small gift (6 d)
Land the Rhine goods on the Stoke bank after dark
Obey the word: sell only English and Frisian goods here
A ship on the sand
Below the town a coaster lies on the sand in the river mouth, canted over, where she has lain since before Michaelmas. Her master stands on the hurdle bank looking at her as a man looks at a debt.

A wide estuary at half tide: a beamy coaster canted over on a sandbank with weed on her waterline, a man on the hurdle bank staring out at her with his arms hanging, a lean fowler in a mud-coloured cloak beside him pointing at a line of withies.
She went on at the top of a spring tide, and every tide beds her deeper. One cable to the far bank and twenty men, and she would come. I have the twenty men.
I ordered sixty fathoms at Dommoc at Lammas and never went for it. A man does not fetch rope he cannot pay for. I do not care to explain that to the rope-maker.
I told him the channel had moved by the second withy. I moved the withy. Nobody else would. He looked at the old mark.
That is her lay. Three strands, hard, tarred at the ends. You brought it on trust? Hers, or yours?
You bought my cable. Well. It was not mine; I had not paid. Will you sell it on, or only show it me?
Hand over the cable and lend your crew to the hauling
Sell him the cable you bought, for half in silver and half in pots
Give him the rope-maker's words, as she said them
Wish him a big tide, and go up to the town
What sings over the houses

Below the town the river widens into shining mud and salt marsh, with one winding channel marked by withies. A lean man in a mud-coloured cloak poles a punt out of a creek with two dead duck in a net bag, and looks at your keel before he looks at you.

A great breadth of shining mud and salt marsh under a wide sky: a lean weathered man in a grey felt cap poling a small punt out of a creek, two duck in a net bag at his feet, a line of withies marking the channel, a skein of swans high overhead.
You came up on the flood without me and touched twice. I heard it from the creek. Next time, a penny, and you touch nothing.
The channel has shifted by the second withy since you were here. I moved the withy. Nobody else would.
My dress is silent when I walk the ground, and sings when the air lifts me over houses. I pass here every winter. Name me. I ask it for nothing.
You have looked up, then. I can see it. Say the name, and say what it is that sings.
The old stone fort at the mouth lost another piece of cliff this winter. Giants built it. Some say a bishop sat there once. I never saw a fire on it.
I do not land at Shotley after dark. I do not say why. My father did not say why either.
The geese came in a week early, flying low. Hard weather behind them, out of the north-east. Lie here a tide longer than you meant to.
Take his riddle away, and watch the sky
Name the bird, and what it is that sings
Pay his penny and follow the punt down
Hear what the geese did this morning, and thank him
The pan, not the face

On the Cornhill a heavy-shouldered Dane with a plaited beard has a folding scale set up on a lime-wood box. He takes a penny, weighs it, bends it, nicks the edge with his knife, and only then looks at the face on it.

A trodden market space with trestles and sacks: a heavy-shouldered fair man with a plaited beard and a nicked silver arm-ring holding a small folding balance over a lime-wood box, a penny in one pan, a merchant waiting with an open purse.
A Frisian. Good. Put your pennies away and put your silver on the scale. Here we believe the pan, not the face.
The man with honest weights. There are two of us in this town now.
The king on this penny is the one we killed. It was thought wiser. A dead king asks very little.
My father said we were given horses here in the first winter. Given. He always smiled at that word. I held them. I was a boy.
The English say no trading on a Sunday or you lose the goods. I have found Monday will do.
You carry your own scale, and you nick before you weigh. Who taught you? No matter. I shall not lean on the pan with you.
A little bronze thing with red eyes went round a child's neck in a hall near here. I know what it was. I do not say whose child.
They are digging a ditch round the town. Against whom, I asked. They looked at me a while.
Sit a morning at his scale and learn the nick and the bend (10 d)
Sell him a cask of wine, weighed out in cut silver (84 d)
Give your opinion of his horse. It is not for sale
The top of the firing

Low round kilns under turf stand at the edge of the town, two of them alight. A red-haired man with clay to the elbows knocks a grey jar with his knuckle, listens to it, and holds it out for you to knock.

Low domed kilns of clay under turf leaking thin grey smoke, rows of unfired jars drying on boards, broken sherds underfoot: a wiry red-haired man with clay to the elbows holding out a grey jar to be knocked, burn scars on both forearms.
Pots? You want pots. Everyone wants pots and nobody says so. Knock on that one. Hear it? That is a sound pot.
The pot man's friend! I kept the top of the last firing for you. The bottom went to the reeve.
The Frisian with the rings says his pots are turned on a fast wheel. So is a drunkard. I build mine to stand.
I send a crate to the bishop's house at Dommoc every Michaelmas. Now I have a pitcher with a spout that pours. Take it up the coast. I want it on a bishop's table.
The bishop poured from it? At table? In front of the abbot? Say it again. Slowly.
The man on the sand is my neighbour. A careful man till this autumn. She will be paid. Tell the rope-maker I shall put in a crate of pots toward it. A handsome crate.
The kilns are cold till Easter. What I have is what there is. Clay will not be hurried, and neither will I.
The wic-reeve has cut the stick for my forty crates? Then I am an honest man on two rivers. Tell the Cornhill. Tell them loudly.
Buy ten crates from the top of the firing (30 d)
Take his pitcher, in a crate, to the bishop at Dommoc
Tell him the bishop poured from it at table
Knock on the pot, and agree that it is sound
The horn-worker's leaf

A gravelled street with a row of timber houses hard on its edge, each with a fenced yard behind. In one a man is boiling horn in a pot that can be smelt from the bank, and beside him on the bench, held down by a horn cup, lies a leaf of writing.

A fenced yard behind a timber house: a craftsman stirring a steaming pot of horn with a stick, polished drinking horns hanging from a rail, a leaf of parchment on the bench weighted with a horn cup, a well lined with dark cask staves in the corner.
Drinking horns, blowing horns, a comb if you are not proud. And that. A clerk owed me for a horn and paid in a leaf. Four pennies and it is yours.
It says: I was a fighter's weapon. Now a young man covers me in silver. Sometimes men kiss me. Sometimes I call friends to the board, sometimes to war. The rest costs.
You have it. Of course you have it; you are standing in it. Say it anyway. I like to hear.
The well there is lined with a wine cask from far up the Rhine. My father sank it. The water still tastes of some bishop's dinner.
You bought my leaf. The fowler has one by heart, and the ale-wife another. Three on one river. Ask them.
Buy the leaf (4 d)
Say what the leaf is about, standing in his yard
Buy a bundle of horn (3 d)
Hold your nose, and pass on
The priest by the ford

A timber church with a shingled roof stands on the rise above the ford, a wooden cross before its door. A slight man with ink on his thumb comes out wiping his hands, dates the morning by a saint, and sighs before he says anything else.

A shingle-roofed timber church on a rise above a river ford, a wooden cross before the door, a fenced graveyard: a slight tonsured priest in an undyed tunic with a wax tablet in his sleeve, bee skeps under a neighbour's eave beyond.
God keep you, shipman. Mass is at the third hour. If you have come for the reeve, he is at the ford; if for God, come in.
You came back safe. I said your name at the altar on Saint Botolph's day. It seems to have been heard.
They say the heathen have killed priests at the altar in the north. I have asked the bishop what we are to do. He has not answered.
This is the month our king was killed, twenty days in. I shall say Mass for a Christian soul. I do not say which, before the clerk. Wax would be a kindness.
A monk who carries Master Alcuin's letters left me a quire of Bede, unfinished. It is where Felix comes to us with his one book. The bishop wants the whole. I have the beginning.
I have a letter for the bishop at Dommoc, and a cold from the last time I walked there. Your boat does not catch cold.
There are barrows under the street by the Cornhill. My grandfather saw them levelled. I say a prayer when I cross it, to be safe.
I say your house's name at the dead king's Mass. I do not say why. The moneyer told me, and then told me he had not.
Your wax burned at the king's Mass. Forty people came up from the bank, and nobody counted them.
You took my letter up the coast. The bishop answered. He never answers me so quickly on foot.
Take his letter to the bishop's house at Dommoc
Give a cake of wax for the dead king's Mass
Take the quire of Bede up the coast for the bishop to see
Hear Mass at the third hour
Forty crates

A moot day on the green outside the town: a single old thorn, a ring of trodden ground, the reeve on a bench carried out for him. The potter stands before it with clay still on his arms. A tally from the Strand at Lundenwic says he owes the toll on forty crates.

A grazed green with a single old thorn tree: a reeve seated on a carried bench holding a notched stick, a red-haired potter before him with clay on his arms and six men in rows behind, townspeople in a ring, rooks overhead.
The wic-reeve on the Strand says forty crates were landed there last year and the toll not paid. The potter says it was. One has a stick. The other has clay on him.
I paid it. Into the hand of a man with a rod, on the hard, in the rain. He cut no stick because his knife was in his other belt. Ask anybody.
You lie on that beach, Frisian. You know how the toll is taken there, and whether a reeve's man ever cuts no stick. Will you stand with him and say so on oath?
Six oath-helpers I have, and all of them potters. The reeve says potters will swear a jar is a horse. One shipman would weigh more than the six.
You stood by me on the green. I do not forget it. Nor does the reeve, who lost a quiet afternoon.
Stand with the potter and swear what you know of the Strand
Offer to ask the wic-reeve himself, next time you lie on the Strand
Say you saw nothing and know less
Eadwynn's bench

A long low house two yards back from the bank, a bush on a pole over the door and a row of straw bee skeps under the south eave. Inside, a Frisian crew sits at one end and potters with clay to the elbow at the other. Eadwynn has a horn dipper in her hand and has already counted your men.

A smoky long alehouse with a hearth in the middle: a tall woman in a green gown with a horn dipper and a ring of keys, potters with clay to the elbows on one bench and a Frisian crew on the other, straw bee skeps seen through the open door.
A new face off a Frisian boat. Sit where I can see you. The first cup is a penny and the second tells me who you are.
You are back, and thinner. Your bench is free. Your man with the laugh, is he still with you?
The potters fire tomorrow. Buy your crates the day after, when they are sober and sorry and the top of the stack is still warm. Not before.
My uncle counted the same boat three times yesterday. Something has come from Tamworth that he does not like.
You have drunk here before, so you may have this. I am carried from groves and hills. I am bound, beaten and drowned, and then I throw old men on their backs.
You have been listening to my bees. Say it, then.
My bees swarmed on the priest's cross at Rogationtide. He blessed them. They stung him. He blessed them again, shorter.
Take her riddle, and listen to the bees
Say what throws old men on their backs
Take her word on the kilns, and buy the day after tomorrow
Take your bench, and tell her Dorestat
Three on one river

By Eadwynn's fire an old sailor sits with his eyes shut, as he has sat every evening you have been in this house. Tonight she touches his shoulder and says three words to him: the bird, the horn, the drink.

A winter evening in a smoky alehouse: an old sailor by the hearth with his eyes shut and his hands on his knees, a tall woman with a horn dipper bending to speak in his ear, the benches gone quiet, snow light at the door.
He will only say it to somebody who has all three. A swan over the roof, a horn at the board, mead on the bench. That is a winter night in a hall.
I can tell a true tale of myself. How I sat the night watch at the stem while she beat along the cliffs, and my feet were bound with frost.
The swan's cry I had for laughter, and the gull's for mead. I am telling you what you answered. Now be quiet, both of you, and I shall tell you what it was for.
There is a man at Dofras has the same poem, they say, and one at Hamwic who ends it differently. He will ask you which is right. Say his, if you want another cup.
Sit down and hear it from the first line
Hear it, and keep him in ale while your lookout learns it (3 d)
Say the tide will not wait for a poem
The wolf pennies
A small strong house with a barred shutter, near the Cornhill. One blow, a pause, one blow. Lul lays down his hammer when he sees the purse in your hand, and weighs you a moment before he weighs it.

A small strong room lit by a barred shutter: a thin dark-haired moneyer with a scorch mark on one cheek holding a single small silver coin up to the light, a she-wolf and two infants just visible on it, his other hand flat over a leather purse on the die block.
Frankish silver? Put it on the pan. It is good silver. It is the wrong king. I shall make it the right one, for my share.
You again, and deniers again. They breed in your purse. Sit; the pot is hot.
Offa's new penny is heavier. A king who adds silver to his coin wants something. I have not yet learned what.
Look, once. A she-wolf feeding two boys, and the word for king. It was on an old coin a pilgrim carried. Somebody thought it would look well. It did.
The dead king's coin is to be brought in and melted. The reeve read it out, slowly. I strike for the Mercian now. A moneyer changes his die.
I kept twelve back. They cannot stay in this house. Take them over the sea, to a pilgrim bound for Rome. Or to the old bishop at Dommoc, who has asked without asking.
They say a moneyer in Lundenwic has a gold piece with marks no priest can read. He copied it and does not know what he wrote. I at least knew it was a wolf.
They are gone where no Mercian will melt them. Do not tell me where. For you the weight and nothing over, while I hold this hammer.
Take the purse of twelve
Change a purse of deniers at his rate (the fire takes 5 d)
Tell him you would sooner see them in his pot than in your boat
Have your purse weighed, and say nothing about kings
The dies and the boy

Half the houses by the Cornhill have new thatch and half have none. At the moneyer's bench Leofsige strikes the town's share of the tribute, one blow at a time, and a boy sweeping the floor behind him looks up at every sail.

A moneyer at his block by rushlight, stooped, a heap of new pennies beside him and an open chest half full, a boy with a broom at the unbarred shutter looking out at a river, half-thatched houses beyond.
Ten thousand pounds, the first time. I strike some of it. A penny looks the same going to a Dane as to a baker.
They will come again. When they do I want my dies and my son out of a town with a mint in it. His mother's brother has boats at Dommoc.
I can sweep, and I can count, and I am not afraid of boats. I am not. I have been in one.
Or put in toward the town's share, as a man with custom here should. Either would be remembered. I do not say which the more.
The boy is safe on the cliff and the spare dies with him. I shall change yours at the weight. The king can spare it; he has spared so much else.
Take the boy and the box of dies to his uncle at Dommoc
Put forty pennies into the town's share
Say you are a Frisian, and count casks
The notched post

Where the track comes down through the chalk bank there is a hurdle fence, a bench, and a post with a notch for every ship of the season. The toll man had counted your strakes before your keel touched.

A low white chalk bank above a shingle strand: a lean grey-haired man on a bench by a hurdle fence with tally sticks in his belt and a small balance in a wooden case, a tall post cut with notches beside him, a boy holding a horse, hulls lying on their bilges below.
A Frisian, by the stem. You lie here, you pay here. By the ship, not by what is in her. I look inside only if you make me.
I have you on the post already. Third notch from the top, the small one. Who is king where you came from?
The Franks' king has shut his shores to our keels, so ours are shut to his. You are his man or you are not. Think before the reeve asks.
The abbess has three ships free by the old king's word. I count four crosses on four stems each summer. I am told my counting is at fault.
My wife's brother is on the strand today in his green cloak. He will ask whose man you are. Then he will ask again. Give him the same answer.
They say the priest who calls himself king had his hair cut for God once. Kent has had stranger. I take the toll and keep the tallies.
You paid by the ship last time and asked for nothing. Good.
The minster's cross was on your stem last time. I counted you with the nuns. My counting, as you know, is at fault.
Pay the king's toll, by the ship (2 d)
Show the abbess's cross on your stem
Come past at the slack, when he is looking at the other tide
Say you have no pennies till you have sold: let him take it on the sales
Heavier than their sins

At the ferry stakes three men in travel-stained cloaks sit on an upturned boat with their staffs, come over from Canterbury for the thresholds of the Apostles. One has his arm over a tight bundle. The ferryman points at it with his pole and laughs.

A line of stakes running out over grey mud to a flat ferry boat at evening: three cloaked men with staffs sitting on an upturned boat, one with his arm over a tight bundle, a short strong ferryman with a cow's horn on a cord pointing at it with a long pole.
Three for Rome, with staffs and one bundle between them. I carried it over on my back. It was heavier than their sins, I can tell you, and I have not seen their sins.
We have no silver but our prayers and our hands at the oars. We ask a passage to the wic on the Canche. God will know your name.
The bundle is bedding. A man sleeps cold on the road to Rome. Twelve blankets is not so many, for three.
They have letters in a Christ Church hand, all three. I cannot read. I can count, and I counted the scribe's face when the third was asked for. It was a long face.
The boatman at Dofras says the inside passage is for men afraid of the Foreland. I say it is for men who mean to arrive.
You took a share of that bundle once. I said nothing to the toll man. I said it to my sister, which is the same thing a week later.
Carry all three for nothing, and ask no questions
Ask what the bundle fetches at Saint-Denis, and take a fifth for your silence
Tell the toll man what is in the bundle
Say you are not bound for the Canche
Tidburh's oysters

A long thatched house stands end-on to the wind, halfway up the bank, with a heap of oyster shells by the door higher than a child. Tidburh is opening oysters with a short knife and does not stop to look at who has come in. She knows the step.

A thatched alehouse interior with a hearth on the floor and a gaming board of yellow bone counters on a bench: a tall spare woman in a linen head-cloth opening oysters with a short knife, a heap of shells by the open door, the brown strait beyond.
Sit by the door, your boots are the strand's. Ale is the island's barley. Wine is for the abbess and for God, in that order.
You came back, so Lundenwic did not eat you. What was wheat there? Tell me true and the first cup is mine to give.
Here is the island's own. The sea fed me and the waves covered me. I have no feet. A man tears my side open with a knife point and eats me raw.
You have the look of a man who has eaten the answer. Say it, and say what speaks without a mouth.
My man went out by the North-mouth at Lammas tide nine summers back, with corn for the Strand. If you hear of a ship called the Sheldrake, tell me. Whatever it is.
The duck's head is on the shelf, facing the door. I talk to it. It answers about as much as he did.
If you lie at the Franks' wic on the Canche, ask for Wulfgifu's house. Say Tidburh still has the blue cup and has not broken it.
Salt is up. The pans at Minster lost a week to rain, and every boat wants it before the herring. Buy today or do not complain to me.
Eat her oysters, and take the riddle with them (1 d)
Say what was fed by the sea and is eaten raw
Promise to ask on the Strand for the Sheldrake
Tell her true what wheat fetched at Lundenwic
The Sheldrake
You are back at the crossing with a carved duck's head wrapped in a cloth. Tidburh is opening oysters, and asks what wheat was at Lundenwic. Her brother is talking, as he always is.

An alehouse bench by the door: a merchant with a cloth-wrapped bundle on his knee, a tall woman pausing with an oyster knife in her hand, a short broad ferryman stopped in the middle of a gesture, grey light off the water through the doorway.
You have something to say, and you are holding your cup with both hands. I have kept this house twenty years. Say it, or say you have nothing.
And so I said to the bishop's man, if you want to be carried dry you must sit still, and he. What is that you have in the cloth?
You told me he sold her sound in the north and went with the buyer. I thanked you. Is there more? There is usually more.
Unwrap the stem-piece, and tell her where the hull was found
Tell her the ship was sold sound in the north, and her man went with the buyer
Say wheat was dear, and keep the cloth shut
Wine for the altar

A long shed of split oak stands at the north end of the strand, a wooden cross nailed over its doors. Inside are oars in a rack, sealed jars and corn in bins, and a small straight-backed nun at a slanted board with a wax tablet, who has heard about you from the toll man.

The wide doors of a split-oak shed with a wooden cross nailed above them, an old patched coaster on rollers outside: a small nun in an undyed gown and dark veil at a slanted board with a wax tablet, oars in a rack and sealed jars behind her.
You are the Frisian. The toll man said small and honest, which from him is praise. Do you carry wine? No? Then sit, and hear what we need.
God's welcome. The last freight tallied to the penny. I mention it because it is rarer than you would think.
No wine, no Mass. A Frankish cask cannot land at Lundenwic this year. It can land here, under our cross, if it is ours when it lands.
The ports are open and the wine comes again, at a price. The altar needs four casks before Easter, whatever kings are doing.
The charter says a ship broken, worn out with great age, or lost by wreck, which God forbid, may be replaced. Ours is two of those already.
The abbess keeps Saint Mildrith's day a fortnight after Saint Peter's. The whole island comes. Bring wax before it and name your price, within reason.
You took our order for wine. The cellaress has washed the jars twice. I told her washing does not bring a ship in.
Take the minster's order: four casks of wine before Easter
Sell her a cask now, landed under the minster's cross (95 d)
Sell her two cakes of wax for the saint's day (90 d)
Hear the charter through, clause by clause
Who weighs with an emperor

Long strips of brown and green run up from the marsh edge to the foot of the down. Eight oxen stand in the furrow. The ploughman has sat down on the headland with a stone like a small loaf in one hand and something small and green in the other.

A brown furrow under a green down in spring light: a long bony ploughman sitting on the headland holding up a tiny green balance by its chain, eight oxen standing in their yokes, small round weights laid out on a flat stone, gulls behind.
A man from over the water. Good. Tell me this. I go nose down and am driven by my enemy, and what I tear, he sows. What am I?
The Frisian. I have a harder one now. Sit on the headland. The oxen want a rest and so do I.
You may take the whole of that one with you. It has more to it: where my lord walks behind me, and what I leave green on one side and black on the other.
I turned up a little pan of green bronze on a chain, and weights with it: old emperors' heads, rubbed flat. Who weighs with an emperor? The priest says bury it.
You have the little pan. Does it weigh true? Then the dead man was honest, whoever he was. That is something to know about a neighbour.
They lie facing east with their swords, waiting for a king who is not coming. We plough round them.
Take the whole riddle of his tool away with you
Buy the little scale and its weights (24 d)
Pay for a Mass at the cross, and have it laid back in the down (6 d)
Sit on the headland and trade him a riddle of your own
Saint Mildrith's day

It is the week of Saint Mildrith. On her day the landing is nearly empty: the whole island has walked to Minster with candles, behind a cross. Only the toll man's boy is left at the cross above the strand, and a nun with the ship-house keys, who is out of temper at having drawn the short straw.

A tall wooden cross on the lip of a chalk bank above an empty strand: a nun with a ring of keys sitting on the flat stone at its foot, far off across green cornland a procession with a cross and candles walking toward a church, the strait shining below.
Every year the island walks to her church, and every year somebody must stay with the keys. The abbess says it is an honour. The abbess is at the feast.
They carry candles to her tomb, in the church Abbess Eadburh built. A candle for the saint from over the sea would be talked of on this island till Martinmas.
Nobody will buy or sell on the strand today. If you cry your wares the island will remember it, and not in the way you want.
At Ebbsfleet they show a rock with her footprint in it, where she stepped ashore from the Franks' land. I have seen it. It is a small foot. She was not a large saint.
Your candle burned before her through the octave last year. I trimmed it myself, and told her whose it was.
Give a cake of wax for a candle at her tomb
Give the price of a candle (6 d)
Walk to Minster after the island, and hear the Mass
Cry your wares on the empty strand
Three keels, still loaded

From the bare green shoulder above the landing the whole strait lies open from mouth to mouth, and the sea beyond the Foreland. Bynna has left his oxen and come up to look, with his hand over his eyes. He counts aloud.

A bare green chalk hilltop with shallow dips in the turf in rows: a long bony ploughman with an ox goad over his shoulder shading his eyes, far below a brown strait with three deep-laden ships coming down it under sail, cornfields and the sea beyond.
Three keels coming back down from the North-mouth, low in the water. Franks, by the cut of them. Nobody comes home from Lundenwic loaded unless he was not let land.
So there is wine in the river that the Strand did not get. A man with wine in his own boat would know what that does to a price. I only plough.
From here I can tell a trader's sail from the other kind. The toll man cannot see past his post. He asks me, and gives me nothing for it. You may give me something.
You paid for my eyes once. They are still good. Look: two more, the same way.
Give him a penny for his eyes, and think about Lundenwic
Look for yourself, and say nothing
Tatwine's leaf

Up the track and inside the city wall, off the archbishop's hall, is a room with a north light: four men at sloped boards, a calfskin stretched on a frame by the door. The thinnest of them speaks without looking up.

A plain room with a north light: four tonsured men at sloped writing boards with quills, a fifth ruling lines with a point, a calfskin stretched on a frame by the door, a thin stooped scribe with ink to the knuckles holding out a leaf without looking up.
Shut the door, the wind is on my neck. You want a leaf, a letter read, or a book carried. Which? I have lost the light already.
You again, and still no calfskin. A book is a herd of calves, merchant. Bring me the herd and I shall show you the book.
The old archbishop made forty riddles. This leaf is one: a thing that guards its master, and is kept in a house it does not own. Fourteen pennies. I read it out once.
Answer it at the hythe, to the reeve's face, and see what he does with your tally. It is a custom. Do not ask who began it.
You have no Latin. Then somebody must read it to you each time you forget it, and you will forget it. Take a reader aboard, or take the one with the short words.
The wic-reeve's two lines about ice? Say them. Yes. The archbishop needed snow, hail and ice together for that. Let me write the English under his Latin. It will annoy somebody.
When the heathen take a book they keep the cover and throw the words in the sea. I think of that when the ink will not flow.
Buy the leaf of the thing and its house (14 d)
Buy the leaf of snow, hail and ice (12 d)
Shut the door behind you, quietly
A herd of calves

The scribe has come out of the writing room into the porch, where the light is better, and is holding a skin up to the sky with both hands. He turns it, finds the scar, and says a short word in Latin.

The south porch of a plain stone church: a thin scribe in a patched black habit holding a pale calfskin up to the sky with both hands, a penknife and a quill behind his ear, a boy with inky arms keeping well back.
Look at that. A fly bit this calf in its first summer, and now there is a hole in Saint Matthew. I need thirty skins without a mark before winter.
Bring them, and I shall count for you what a gospel book costs: the skins, the months, the gold. Then you will know what a heathen has in his hand.
The hayward on the mares' marsh knows who has calves and who has only promises. He will tell you in one sentence. Wait for it.
Those are calf? Unscarred? Lay them on the bench. Do not let the boy touch them; he has ink on him to the elbow.
You took my order for skins. I have ruled the first quire on trust. Do not make me scrape it.
Take his order: six bundles of clean calfskin before winter
Lay six bundles of skins on his bench, and be taught what a book is worth
Tell him calves are no cargo for a small boat
Leaves kept dry
You have come up the track with something sealed under your cloak. In the porch of Christ Church the scribe holds out an inky hand for it before you have said whose it is.

A church porch in grey light: a thin inky scribe holding out his hand, a merchant drawing a sealed leaf from under his cloak, a clerk's boy with a wax tablet looking on, the track running away downhill toward marsh and a river.
That is Eanwulf's hand, from Saint Paul's. He wants a book, as usual, and has bad news, as usual. I shall read it standing up.
An oath from the East Angles' new bishop. The Trinity, the fire, obedience all his days. His own hand, and a good one. Where is Dommoc? No, do not tell the archbishop I asked.
Leaves travel worse than wine and are worth more. You kept them dry. Most do not; they come in smelling of the bilge.
Hand over the letter from Saint Paul's
Hand over the bishop of Dommoc's oath
Keep them under your cloak a while longer
The blank tally

A bench under a lean-to of hurdles stands at the head of the hythe, with a peg-board behind it hung with tally sticks. A heavy man with a white wand sits counting on his fingers, where you can see him do it.

A low gravel river bank among reeds with boats lying stem-in: a heavy bald reeve on a bench under a hurdle lean-to holding a leaf of parchment upside down, a peg-board of tally sticks behind him with three small painted crosses, a merchant before him.
You lie at the king's hythe, so you pay the king's toll. By the ship. I shall look at her, not in her, unless you give me cause.
Your stick is on the board. Third from the door. The river has dropped a hand since you were here: go out on the big tide.
The Franks have shut their shores to us and we to them. A Frisian is not a Frank. I have decided that. The wic-reeve has not.
The clerks sell riddles. One of the old archbishop's, answered to my face, passes a ship free. Have you a leaf? Hold it up. I cannot read it. I know it by the shape.
Last time you gave me a bought answer. I know one by how it is said: quickly, like a man putting down something hot. What is the thing's house made of?
Your stick is the blank one. I hung it myself. Do not tell the clerks how pleased I was; they will raise the price of the leaf.
The cellarer wants wax by Candlemas and does not know it yet. Bring it, and name your price.
Give him the answer to Tatwine's leaf, in your own words
Give him the answer a clerk's boy sold you at the alehouse (2 d)
Pay the toll, by the ship
Eoba's bench

In a lane off the market inside the wall stand three open-fronted sheds, each with a stump of oak and a die standing in it. A short thick-armed man does not bite your coin. He drops it on the stump and listens to it ring.

A lane of open-fronted sheds inside a flint-and-tile wall: a short thick-armed man in a leather apron dropping a penny on an oak stump with a die set in it, a small balance in a case at his neck, a boy sweeping the floor with a hare's foot.
Frankish silver? Put it on the cloth. I give you the king's new pennies for it, less my share and the fire's. The fire is the greedier.
The Frisian with the honest deniers. Heavier pennies this year, so fewer of them. Do not look at me. I only hold the die.
I struck for the queen, with her face on it. No other moneyer in England has done that. No other queen has asked.
What did Ibba give you on the Strand? So. His letters are better than his sums. They say he copied a gold piece with marks like worm tracks.
When a king dies I keep the old dies under the bench for a season. You would be surprised how often a season is enough.
What have you there? A pan on a chain. And these: emperors, rubbed flat. That one is the weight of the gold piece. That one is the Danes' ounce. Leave them till the bell.
You know what each weight is for now. Nick before you weigh, bend before you trust. In the north they will stop leaning on the pan.
Leave the old weights with him till the bell, and be taught them
Bring him your strange silver first, unweighed (he takes 2 d)
Let him ring a penny on the stump, and listen
Ten in the yard

Between the fences and the water, goods stand as they come off the boats. A broad red-armed woman sits among them with a withy cage of hens on one side and a basket on the other, and has counted your crew before you have counted her eggs.

A strip of gravel between wattle fences and a brown river: a broad red-armed woman in a linen head-cloth sitting with a withy cage of hens and a basket of eggs, querns in straw and tied jars around her, a monk's ox cart waiting behind.
Eggs, child, laid this morning, and a cheese that will see you to the Franks' shore. You are thin. They do not feed you on that boat.
There he is. Four of you still, and the big quiet one? Good. I kept the brown hen's eggs back. I said he will come on the tide.
The reeve has owed me for eggs since the old king's day. I keep the stick. One of us will die first, and I mean it to be him.
You have bought of me before, so you may have this. Ten of them in the yard, child, with their coats hung on the wall. What walked out?
My cousin at the Sarre crossing says four ships passed with crosses on them. The abbess has three. Somebody cannot count, or somebody can.
The clerks pay for the white of the egg and throw the yolk away. For gilding, they say. I have six children fed on what Christ Church throws away.
Buy eggs and two cheeses for the crew (3 d)
Take the riddle of the ten in the yard
Count the notches on her egg stick aloud, where the reeve can hear
Tell her the boat feeds you well enough
Blow a horn

East of the plots the land lies flat and green to a line of willows, mares and foals standing in it to their hocks. You have left the track to look at them. A tall man with a long wooden rake and a cow's horn on a thong is walking toward you, not quickly.

A flat wet meadow cut by black ditches under a wide grey sky, mares and foals standing to their hocks: a tall lean man in a hooded cape of undyed wool walking toward the viewer with a long wooden rake, a cow's horn on a thong at his belt.
Track is there. You are here. Blow a horn or go back to it.
The Frisian. Mind the ditch.
A stranger off the track, no shout, no horn: the old king's law says thief. I say it too. But I look first.
It noses the ground and has more teeth than a hound. It bites nothing. It feeds my beasts all winter. I am holding it.
Calves. The farm on the rise. Thin skins, no fly. He will say twelve pennies the bundle. Say ten. Then be quiet. That is all.
Rain by the second tide. Go now.
Blow your steersman's horn, badly, and stay where you are
Take the riddle of the thing he is holding
Buy six bundles of calfskin at the farm on the rise, at ten the bundle (60 d)
What is in a man's bundle

In the south porch of Christ Church three men with staffs and wallets wait their turn. One wears a better cloak than a pilgrim should own, and has a tight bundle between his feet. Through the open door the scribe writes two letters without looking up, and stops at the third.

The south porch of a stone church in grey morning light: three men with staffs and wallets waiting, one in a better cloak with a tight bundle between his feet, and through the open door a thin monk at a sloped board, writing, not looking up.
