Letters of passage for the thresholds of the Apostles. Two I have written. The third man: what does a pilgrim want with twelve cloaks? You carry such men, shipman. Tell me.
A word in your ear. I have cloth the Franks would pay double for, and no way to land it but on a pilgrim's back. Say you know me. A fifth is yours.
A true pilgrim crosses free, by the Frankish king's word. The archbishop seals what I write. He cannot seal what is in a man's bundle, and one day he will be asked.
You vouched for a cloth dealer in this porch once. I wrote what you said. I have not forgotten whose word it was.
You told me plainly once that you did not know a man. The archbishop's count is clean because of it.
Tell the scribe plainly that you do not know the man
Vouch for him, and take a fifth (24 d)
Say it is no business of a Frisian's
The abbey of the kings' graves

Outside the east wall of the city, inside a bank and a gate of its own, two stone churches stand in a line. In the older one the first archbishops lie along the north side and the kings of Kent along the south. A porter with a bunch of keys looks at your shoes.

A gate in a bank with two plain stone churches in a line beyond it and a paved yard between: a porter in a dark habit with a bunch of keys looking down at a merchant's muddy shoes, a long shuttered building behind where the books are kept.
Thanks be to God. Who knocks? A shipman. Wipe your feet on the grass; these stones have had kings on them.
Three nights, bread and ale, and no meat on a fast. The brothers will ask you for news and give you none. That is the Rule.
One of your men is grey in the face. The brother who keeps the sick has herbs and an opinion. Bring him in. The house does not refuse a gift.
You carry a leaf you cannot read? A brother reads for guests after the ninth hour. He will tell you what it says, and what it does not.
In the chest is a king's gift of land over the ford, in the hand that first wrote it. They show it to guests who can be trusted not to breathe on it.
Lodge the crew three nights at the guest house (alms of 4 d)
Bring your sick man to the brother who keeps the sick (6 d)
Ask a brother to read your leaf
Stand a while among the kings, and go
A little more than last time

A stout man with a long moustache and rings on two fingers meets your keel with his arms wide. He knew your father's stem before he saw your face, he says. Then he names the customs, and they are a little more than last time.

A row of narrow fenced plots running down to a river: a stout clean-shaven man with a long moustache, a fur-edged cloak and a staff of office, arms spread in welcome, one hand resting on a purse, a foreign keel nosing the bank behind him.
A keel from over the sea! Welcome. You lie on the abbot's land now, by the king's gift, so you pay the abbot. Through me.
I knew your father's stem before I saw your face. The customs have gone up a little. Everything has. Sit, drink first.
The men of Dofras go quit of toll through all England, they say. So they do. I toll them, and give it back when a steersman comes for it with the hall behind him.
The port-reeve in London writes to ask what the men of Rouen paid here. I write back about the weather. We understand each other.
You put me to my oath before the shire. I do not hold it against you. I hold very little; that was the finding.
Between us: some of what I took from your house I took unjustly. I may yet have to swear to it. Better I give it back first.
Pay what he names (12 d over the lawful toll)
Put him to his oath before the shire, with two witnesses
Ask, as a friend, for what he took unjustly
Lay the lawful toll on his bench and say nothing more
Nine for the Apostles

Nine people sit on the shingle above the weed line with staffs and wallets, waiting for a boat to the Franks' shore. Wulfric stands a little way off with his eyes on the water. He does not turn his head to tell you about them.

A steep bank of shingle in a gap between white cliffs: nine cloaked people with staffs sitting in a row above the weed line, one with a tight square bundle under his knees, a short thick boatman with a bailing scoop at his belt looking out to sea, a pale line of far shore.
Nine on the shingle say they go to the Apostles. Seven walk like pilgrims. Two walk like men who have carried cloth all their lives.
We have no silver, shipman, only prayers and our hands at the oars. Set us down at the wic on the Canche and God will know your boat.
A word apart. Thirty cloaks pass as one man's bedding if nobody lifts the corner. A third of what they fetch is yours, and nothing said on either shore.
My sister lodges people over there. She says the toll men open every bundle now. She also says the abbot has not said no. With her that is good news.
The cloth in that bundle was woven under the west wall. The woman who wove it gets the half. Ask her what she thinks of pilgrims.
You took a bundle over under the thwarts once. I saw how she sat on the stones: a hand lower than nine thin men make her.
You took the cloth over declared. My sister sold it by daylight. She says that is rarer than a fair wind in Lent.
Carry the seven free, and take the cloaks over as the weaver's own goods, declared
Carry all nine, bundle and all, for a third of the sale (60 d)
Go up to the south gate and tell the reeve whose bundle it is
Take the seven who walk like pilgrims, and leave the bundle on the stones
A priest for Rome

Among those waiting on the shingle is a young priest with an East Anglian way of speaking and a staff cut from a thorn. Wulfric has told him where your boat last lay. He looks at your purse as if he knew what was in it, and then you see that he does.

Shingle at first light under white cliffs: a young tonsured priest with a thorn staff holding a single small silver coin in his open palm and weeping, a merchant with an open purse, a short boatman turned politely away toward the water.
You are from the Orwell? I was a boy on the bench at Dommoc. Abbot Lull beat nobody and I learned anyway. Have you news of my country that can be said aloud?
That is his penny. The wolf and the two boys. I saw him ride in at Easter when I was twelve. They cut off his head, and now they melt his name.
Give them to me and I swear by Saint Peter's own door that one shall lie at his threshold. Rome keeps what England is told to forget.
He has asked every keel for nine tides. He has no fare. He prays loudly, and it is not for a wind.
Put the purse in his hand, and take nothing for it
Give him the purse, and a passage to the Canche with it
Give him eleven, and keep the twelfth in your own chest
Keep the purse shut for now
Bread at the south door

Inside the old wall a wooden church stands among timber houses, and at its south door there is a line: women with bowls, an old man led by a child, two families off the downs with nothing in their hands. A thin canon with tally sticks under his arm is counting loaves, and has too few.

The south door of a wooden minster inside a tall wall of flint and red tile: a line of thin people with bowls, a lean grey-tonsured canon with notched hazel sticks under his arm handing out half loaves from a basket, a merchant standing at the end of the line.
The harvest failed here too. I break each loaf in two now, and next week in three. Saint Martin divided his cloak. He was not asked to divide it forty ways.
Is that barley in your boat? Then hear me before the men at the gate do. They will give ten pennies the sack and sell at twenty. I can give four and a blessing.
The Franks' king has set a price on corn, they say, so that no man grows fat on a hungry year. Ours has not. So it is left to each man with a sack.
Your barley fed that door for nine days. Your name is in our book, among those we pray for at Martinmas. I wrote it myself, and I spell well.
You sold at the gate. It was your corn. I say nothing; I only count who stands in my line, and it is longer.
Give two sacks of barley at the south door
Sell him four sacks at last year's price (16 d)
Sell four sacks to the men at the gate, at this year's price (40 d)
Stand a moment at the end of the line, and go
The chest under the red floor

Cynehelm shuts the church door behind you and drops the bar himself. In the half dark by the altar stands a mud-splashed clerk you have not seen before, and at his feet an iron-bound chest with a mule's pack-rope still round it.

The dim inside of a wooden church with a smooth dark red floor: a thin canon dropping the bar across the door, a mud-splashed young clerk standing over an iron-bound chest with a pack-rope round it, one candle, a merchant between them.
This man came over the downs by night with a mule. In the chest are a gospel book, a psalter and the church's charters. The archbishop has gone another way.
My lord was King Offa's man, and since the summer Kent has a king of its own again. I do not ask you to love either. I ask you to carry a box.
I can put it under this floor. But the church is wood, the town is wood, and one spark is enough. I want it over the water, with Master Alcuin's monks at Saint Josse.
Wulfric will not take it; his boat is known. A Frisian keel is nobody's business. He will show you the hour of the tide and say nothing after.
A man of the new king's sits at the reeve's bench. He pays for news of anything that was the archbishop's. I tell you, so that you know what I know you know.
Take the clerk and the chest over the water to Saint Josse, and ask no fee
Help Cynehelm lift the red floor, and say nothing after
Go to the man at the reeve's bench (120 d)
Say this is Kent's quarrel, and no Frisian's
Hildgyth's looms

Under the west wall stands a row of sunk huts with their doors open for the light, and in each a loom leaning on the wall with its clay rings swinging. In the nearest a strong-armed woman beats the weft up with a bone sword, and does not stop when your shadow falls on the cloth.

A row of sunk-floored huts under a tall flint-and-tile wall, doors open: a strong-armed woman in a russet gown at an upright loom hung with clay rings, a bone weaving-sword in her hand, wool fluff on everything, folded cloaks stacked on a bench, daughters at three more looms.
Feel that. Go on, with your thumb. That is two fleeces and eleven days. Now, what do they give for it at Dorestat? Do not lie.
You came back, so you sold them. What did the Frisians say about the length? Too short, I suppose. Everyone is a king now.
The Franks' king says our cloaks will not cover him in bed nor keep the rain off him on a horse. Let him ride less.
One of those pilgrims on the stones has thirty of my cloaks in his bundle and a psalm on his lips. I would sooner a Frisian carried them openly.
My cousin Leofrun weaves on the Strand at Lundenwic. Ask her why the Franks want them longer. She will not know either, but she will have asked more people.
Leofrun says she asked first? She always did. So: the wool of a cloak and a third, and half on the chest before the shuttle moves. I can cut to that.
You took five of mine over as mine. What did they fetch? The true price, mind. I have Wulfric's sister's word to set beside yours.
I cut to the Frankish length now, for those who ask. Feel the weight of it. That is a king's complaint, answered in wool.
You brought back the true price. Most bring back a story. Sit; the girls will find you something to eat.
Buy four cloaks at the loom's price (56 d)
Lay the price of her five cloaks on the bench (70 d)
Give her Leofrun's answer, and the measure on a knotted cord
Tell her true what Dorestat gives, and take her question to the Strand
The long song

Beornflaed's house is built against the old wall, which holds the heat. Everybody who waits for a wind waits here. By the hearth sits an old man with a thorn staff across his knees, half speaking and half chanting to nobody, and the bench nearest him is left empty out of respect or caution.

A crowded alehouse built against a wall of flint and red tile: an old man with white hair to the shoulder and a thorn staff across his knees by the hearth, his mouth open in a chant, a broad upright woman with a wooden ladle watching him, travellers on the benches gone quiet.
Sit by the old wall, it holds the heat. Two nights you are a guest. The third night I answer for you, so tell me now what you are.
There you are. Your bench is free. What are they saying at Dorestat? I have people waiting to hear.
The old man will tell the long song for an evening's ale. The house goes quiet for it. I never ask it to.
I can make a true song of myself. Nights at the stem under the cliffs, my feet bound with frost, and hunger tearing a sea-weary man from within. You know the start.
I stand on a cliff and showed ships their road. My eye is out, and they steer by me still. Say what I am. No, do not say. Climb up tomorrow and look.
They tell me a man at Hamwic ends it another way. He is a West Saxon. They end everything another way.
You have the song now. Say it on the night watch, and slowly. It was not made for men in a hurry.
You kept him in ale a whole evening and my house in quiet. I sold more that night than at Martinmas.
Keep him in ale for the evening, and hear the whole song (3 d)
Buy him one cup, and hear the start of it (1 d)
Sit by the old wall and tell her Dorestat
The tower with no fire

On the height east of the town an eight-sided tower of flint and red tile stands as tall as four houses, with jackdaws going in and out where the fire used to be. At its foot, out of the wind, sits old Lulla with his staff, counting sails.

A tall eight-sided tower of flint banded with red tile on a green cliff top, jackdaws wheeling from its open crown: an old man in a patched sheepskin sitting at its foot with a thorn staff, pale eyes on the strait, a far shore sharp and white across the water.
I saw you come in from the top. You held too far east and the stream carried you right. That is luck or knowledge. Which?
The Frisian with the brown sail. I knew you at the Foreland. Sit. I will tell you what else is out there.
Three sails went west under the far shore at first light, close together, low in the water. Not fishermen. I did not like their keeping together.
The far cliffs stand up sharp as a knife this morning. When you can count the Franks' sheep, do not sail. Rain by dark, wind after.
The clerk says Romans built it. My grandfather said giants. Nobody alive could, so what is the difference? Jackdaws keep it now.
Your fire burned all last night. Two boats came in on it that would have gone by. They do not know whose it was. I do.
I lifted the staff. You did not look back. Well, you are here, so the sea was kinder than I would have been.
Sit the morning out with him, and wait for his word on the wind
Sail now, against his word
Pay for a watch fire beside the tower, and a man to burn it (200 d)
Carry a jug up the hill for him (1 d)
The king's peace

The herring boats are out, and the king's peace lies on the town. On the shingle one of your men and a Boulogne shipman have come to blows over whose rollers are whose. A square weathered man with a steersman's horn at his back walks down from the hall, not hurrying.

A shingle beach crowded with herring boats and drying nets under white cliffs: a square weathered man with a horn slung at his back standing between a Frisian crewman and a furious Frankish shipman holding his jaw, townsmen gathering, a timber hall above.
From Michaelmas to Saint Andrew the king's peace lies on this town. Break it now and the reeve takes the fine from everyone alike. Yours and his.
Your man struck first. I have a tooth to show for it, and it is not in my mouth.
We give the king twenty ships for fifteen days, and carry his messengers over. For that we go quit of toll through all England. You do not live here. So you pay.
Settle it on the stones and the hall need never hear. Take it to the hall and the hall hears all of it, and so does the reeve.
The hall found for you, and the Boulogne man paid. Do not make a habit of being right in my town.
You hauled his boat up yourself last time. It was talked of. Not unkindly.
Pay the Boulogne man for his tooth, here on the stones (8 d)
Take it before the hall, with your crew as witnesses
Put your own shoulder to his boat and haul her up, as amends
A pole in the haven

North of the cliff a river comes out through shingle banks into the sea, and inside the mouth boats lie on the mud. A broad bow-legged man in a tarred hood wades out with a sounding pole taller than himself, looking at the sky, and names your boat before he names you.

A river mouth between shingle banks under a low cliff of sand with a small church on it: a broad bow-legged man in a tarred hood and a sealskin apron wading out with a tall sounding pole, small boats on the mud behind him, grey sea, a thorn tree on the cliff.
A Dorestat boat, clinker, six oars. I had you from the cliff. Come in on my pole; the bank has shifted since Easter.
You. Same boat, new patch on the sail. Lay her where you lay last time. I have kept the place.
A Gipeswic master ordered rope from my wife's sister at Lammas and has not come for it. Ask her. Do not ask her loudly.
The cliff lost a cart's length this winter. My father's father ploughed where you are floating.
Wind is going north-east by morning. You may not believe me today. You will tomorrow.
Since the news from the north I look twice at any sail I cannot name. I named yours. Be glad of it.
I told my wife's sister that you pay in full. Do not make me a liar. She would enjoy it too much.
Pay his penny, and come in on his pole
Buy a barrel of his salt herring (10 d)
Feel your own way in, slowly, and thank him
Three questions

On the shingle under the cliff, where the market is, a tall young man in a red cloak leans on a spear and watches your keel touch. His riding boots are ruined with salt. He lets you get one foot on the stones before he speaks.

A shingle strand under a cliff of sand, a few trestles and baskets: a tall fair-moustached young man in a red cloak with a silver disc brooch leaning on a spear, good riding boots white with salt, a Frisian master stepping ashore before him, fishermen watching sideways.
Stand there. Whose ship is that, whose man are you, and from which shore? I ask three times. It is the king's way.
The Frisian. I have your answers by heart. Give me a new one: what is wine fetching across the water?
A king's order is like a net. It is made for the large fish. I was not told what to do about the small ones.
King Offa asked the Frank for a daughter and the Frank shut his ports. So I watch a beach. That is statecraft.
You have been looked at on the Strand? Then the wic-reeve cut you a stick. Show it. I know his notch: he cuts deep, like a man who expects to be doubted.
You have leave here. I ask the three questions because I am watched while I ask them. I write nothing down.
You beat me at the pebbles. The ale-wife says I let you. I did not let you.
Show him the wic-reeve's tally from the Strand
Answer with a cask of what is in the hold
Offer him a game at the pebble board, for the toll
Answer all three, three times, and pay what is asked
Wine for the altar

A timber church with a porch of old stone stands near the cliff edge, the sea loud behind it. A small old man in a darned habit comes out to you leaning on a wooden staff with a curled head. He asks after your own saint before he asks what is in your boat.

A timber church with a stone porch near the edge of a sandy cliff, graves in the grass: a small thin old bishop in a plain undyed habit with a curled wooden staff and a worn silver ring, walking a merchant out among the graves, grey sea beyond.
You are from over the sea. God keep you. Have you been north this summer? We hear a thing about Saint Cuthbert's church that I would rather not believe.
The Frisian again. Sit. The boys have been asking whether your boat really has only four men in her.
The Mass wine is nearly gone. I water it more than the canons allow, and so far God has said nothing. A cask would be named at the altar.
Walk out among the graves with me. Our king went to Offa's hall to ask for a daughter. That is all I will say indoors.
Lul at Gipeswic struck pennies for him, with a wolf on them. I should like one by the altar on his day, twenty days into the month of three milkings. I do not ask.
It lies under the altar cloth. I say his name there, quietly. God hears quiet things.
From the potter at Gipeswic? He sends a crate each Michaelmas, and a message with it about tables. Let me see it pour.
Come at Lent if you can. It is our own saint's Mass, and nobody sells us wax for it.
Put one of the dead king's pennies into his hand, out among the graves
Sell him a cask for the altar (80 d)
Set the potter's pitcher on his table
Hear his Mass, with the sea loud behind it
The boys' bench

In the bishop's house six boys sit on one bench with one worn leaf between them, held up by a round red-faced abbot with chalk on his sleeve. He sees you in the doorway and is plainly glad of a reason to stop.

A timber hall with a long bench: six boys in a row squinting at one worn leaf of parchment held up by a round red-faced abbot in a patched black habit, a hazel switch in his other hand pointing at a word, a satchel of wax tablets at his feet.
A merchant. Then you can count. Can you read? No matter, the boys cannot either yet. Sit and tell me a thing I do not know.
My Frisian. I have a question saved for you since the last moon. It has four feet in the morning. No, that is another one.
Honey-bees gave me my inside, the wood my outside, and iron ploughs me. Bishop Aldhelm made it. I will not hear your answer until you have held one in your hand.
You have been to Blythburgh. I can tell: you are looking at my satchel. Say it, then.
The second is footless, fixed to its place, and eaten raw. Look in the cliff under the church. The third stands on high rocks and shows ships their road with fire.
You answered before I had finished. That is rude. Where did you see one? And what did the Orwell fowler tell you about the old stone fort?
There are three Lulls. One was bishop at Mainz and is dead. One strikes the king's pennies. I am the one with no silver.
If you lie at Hamwic, tell the priest of the shore church his cask has a word wrong. I will not say which. It will keep him busy till Easter.
I mean to go over the sea to the great teacher once more before I die. Have you room for a fat abbot who talks?
My letter of greeting is in your chest. Show it to any master on the monks' road. He will set you something harder than I did, to spite me.
Say what the bees, the wood and the iron make
Name the shell and the tower, and tell him what the fowler said of the stone fort
Give the abbot a passage over the sea, toward Tours
Take the first riddle away with you, and his word for Hamwic
A letter up the cliff

You have climbed the cliff path with the Gipeswic priest's letter inside your tunic. At the door of the bishop's house a clerk with a wax tablet takes one look at the seal and sighs like a man who knows the hand.

The door of a timber hall at the top of a steep cliff path: a clerk with a wax tablet at his belt holding out his hand for a small sealed leaf, a merchant out of breath from the climb, the haven and its boats far below.
From Hereberht by the ford? Then it begins with his cold and ends with his bees. The bishop reads them through all the same.
He walks here twice a year and is ill for a month after each. You have saved him one of them.
The new bishop answers a letter the day it comes. It is hard on the rest of us.
Hand over the letter from Gipeswic
Keep it inside your tunic a while longer
The trumpet of God
The new bishop is tall, with mud to the knee and a wax tablet hanging at his belt. He is counting something off on his fingers when you come in, and he finishes counting before he looks up.

A timber hall with a chest and a long bench: a tall strong-jawed bishop in a dark habit under a good riding cloak, mud to the knee, counting on his fingers, a wax tablet and stylus at his belt, a sealed leaf lying on the chest beside him.
A boat from Dorestat. Good. I need three things carried and one thing bought, and I pay for all four.
You came back, and in the week you said. I shall start trusting your boat more than the king's roads.
This leaf is my oath to the archbishop: the Trinity, the judgement by fire, obedience all my days. It must reach Canterbury dry. The landing is called Fordwic, they tell me.
Master Alcuin writes that a bishop's mouth should be the trumpet of God. I read it to the priests. Two of them looked at their feet.
Bede wrote of Felix and of this city. We have not got the book. A see that cannot read its own beginning.
That is Bede? Give it here. Felix, the city Dommoc, seventeen years. So we were a city. Abbot! Set the boys to copy this before the light goes.
Six leaves, sewn into the front of the psalter. A see can begin with less. Felix began with none.
The archbishop has my oath, and one of his clerks asked where Dommoc is. I am told you answered him politely.
Take his oath, sealed, for the archbishop at Canterbury
Lay the quire of Bede on the boys' bench
Sell him two cakes of wax for the altar (88 d)
Hear what was decided at the last council, and say little
Sixty fathoms

Behind the town lies a black pond that can be smelt from the haven, with bundles of hemp weighted under the water and a long straight walk beside it where a pale rope is stretched taut. A strong-armed woman shouts over the crank without turning her head.

A black pond with bundles of hemp stalks weighted under stones, and beside it a long straight rope walk with a pale rope stretched taut on posts: a strong-armed woman with grey cracked hands and a hank of yarn over her shoulder, a child turning a crank, a great tarred coil in an open shed.
Mind the pond. If you have come to say it stinks, I know. If you have come for rope, feel that and tell me I am wrong.
The Frisian with the small boat. Did my rope hold? Then say so in Gipeswic, where they pretend theirs is as good.
Sixty fathoms of cable lying in my shed since Lammas. Three strands, hard laid, tarred at the ends. A Gipeswic man's word is worth less than his rope, and I made his rope.
I want my price, eighty pennies, or the man's reason. I would rather have both.
The pilot says you pay in full. He says it of four men on this coast, and one of them is dead. Take it on a tally, then.
On the sand since before Michaelmas? Then he is a fool and not a thief. A fool I can deal with. The cable is here, and the price has not gone down.
He paid in full at the next moon, and sent a crate of pots. They are ugly. They are on my shelf. For you the maker's price, while I pull hemp.
You sold him my cable yourself? A fair trade, and I say so. He is afloat, I hear. When he orders again he pays first.
Hemp hangs the thief and holds the ship. One field, two trades.
Take the cable to Gipeswic on her tally
Pay her price, and take the cable for your own (80 d)
Buy six coils at the maker's price (48 d)
Promise to ask at Gipeswic for the man's reason
Tidswith's board

At the top of the cliff path is a low house with a bush over the door and a bench that looks out to sea. Inside, a small quick woman in a yellow head-cloth has a jug in her hand and a bunch of wooden tallies at her waist, and has already seen that you looked at the door before you sat.

A low alehouse at the top of a steep cliff path, the sea far below through the open door: a small quick dark-haired woman in a yellow head-cloth and a striped apron with a jug, wooden tallies on a thong at her waist, a board marked in squares with pebbles on it.
Ale is a farthing's worth a cup, or four for a cut penny. News costs more. Sit where you can see the door.
You drink slow and you pay. I kept your cup. The corner seat is the pilot's; any other.
A man in from the north sat there and did not speak for two cups. Then he said the heathens took the boys as well.
The Mercian comes every evening to watch the door for enemies of the king. He has been watching my jug.
The Mercian wants one of the dead king's pennies, to show at Offa's hall who is still prayed for here. He would give sixty for it. I only tell you what was said.
Malt is dear and getting dearer. If you carry barley, come to me before you go down to the strand.
A Gipeswic pilot will tell you Felix sat in the old stone fort by the Orwell, not on this cliff. Do not say it in here. The bishop's cook drinks here.
There is a game here with pebbles on a board. I beat the Mercian at it. He thinks he lets me.
Sell her three sacks of barley before the strand sees them (15 d)
Sell one wolf penny to the Mercian, through her (60 d)
Buy the silent man from the north a cup, and hear the rest (1 d)
Drink slow, pay, and watch the door
The digger with the white neck

Above the town the fields run to the cliff's edge and stop, with a furrow or two hanging over nothing. A man with a bundle of snares and two hares at his belt is looking down the cliff face at something, and waves you back from the edge without turning round.

Plough strips running to the crumbling edge of a sandy cliff, heath and gorse behind: a lean man in a hooded leather jerkin with snares over his shoulder and two hares at his belt, pointing down at a dark band of shells and red sherds in the cliff face.
Mind the edge, shipman. It was a cart's length further out when I set these snares.
My neck is white and my head is dun. I go fast on my toes, and I dig a road through the steep hill for my children when the hound comes. What am I?
You have been thinking about it at sea. I can tell. Say it.
See the dark band in the cliff, with the oyster shells and the red sherds? Somebody ate here before the English. Nobody knows who. They ate well.
There is a bunch of little bronze keys sticking out of the ash there. I leave them. A man who takes keys should know the door.
My fire is yours when you lie here. It is not much of a fire, but it is out of the wind.
Take his riddle to sea with you
Name the digger with the white neck
Buy his two hares for the crew's pot (2 d)
Look over the edge at the shells, and step back
The king's grave

A short pull up the river on the flood, a small church stands on a rise above the reeds. Inside it is nearly dark. One lamp burns over a stone slab, and beside it a priest is doing his reckonings on something pale and flat that is not wood.

A small dark timber church on a rise above a reedy river: one lamp burning over a plain stone grave slab, a priest seated beside it writing with a stylus on a pale tablet of whalebone with a row of runes cut along its border.
King Anna lies here, whom the heathen Mercian killed, and his son beside him. Pilgrims come. Not many. The ones who come are in earnest.
This? I keep my reckonings on it. Whalebone, with a wax face. I cut the staves in the border myself, where a Latin scribe would rule lines. Hold it if you like.
The abbot sent you to look at it? He sends them all. He could show them his own. He likes people to walk.
One king of ours killed by a Mercian lies here. Now there is another, and nobody will say where he lies. I light the lamp for both. Do not tell the king's man.
The lamp burns oil when there is oil and tallow when there is not. The king does not complain.
Take the tablet in your hands, and turn it over
Give for the lamp at the king's grave (3 d)
Make a vow at the grave for a safe crossing
Stand a while in the dark, and go back down to the boat
The dies come ashore

The strand below the cliff is silver with fish and loud with gulls, and women are gutting at long trestles. A thick-set man with salt-scarred hands sees the boy on your stem and the box under his arm, and puts down his horn.

A shingle strand heaped with herring, gulls wheeling, women gutting at long trestles: a thick-set man in a hooded cloak stiff with scales, red hands scarred white, staring at a boy who stands in the bow of a small boat clutching a wooden box.
That is my sister's boy, and that is her man's box under his arm. So they have come to Gipeswic again, or he thinks they will. Come up out of the women's way.
I was not sick. I was looking at the water, closely.
My sister's man strikes pennies, and they pay the Danes with them. I catch herring, and the Danes eat that too. One family, feeding one army.
A man who was at Maldon came through at Martinmas. He had it in verse already. Do you want it? It is long, and nobody in it runs who should not.
Hand over the boy and the box, and take nothing but fish
Hand them over, and stay to hear what was done at Maldon
The bishop's seal

The church chest stands open and nearly empty. A spare old man in a faded vestment has a list in one hand, and turns something small over and over in the other: a little cone of bronze on a cord, with red stones that catch the light.

Inside a timber church by a nearly empty open chest: a spare white-tonsured old bishop in a faded dark vestment holding a list in one hand and a small bronze cone-shaped seal on a cord in the other, tiny red stones glinting, grey light from the door.
A merchant, in this year. Either you are brave or nobody has told you. Come in. I have an errand that needs a man nobody is watching.
They wintered among us and we gave them horses. A man who has your horses will come back for your saddle.
The books have gone to Hoxne, where the church has land. The plate is in the pond under the hemp, where no man will put his arm. This I kept a while longer.
It is my seal. Two rows of little arches, a beast's head in each. Take it up the river road to the island by Hoxne. Give it to the priest, or to the ground.
The king is dead. I am the fourteenth or the fifteenth since Felix. The list has a gap, and I could not mend it. Soon it will not matter.
Write the name down. What is written can be lost, but what is not written is lost already.
Take the seal inland, to the priest by Hoxne or to the ground
Take it, and sell it to the army's buyers as bronze and red stones (40 d)
Refuse the seal, and offer him a passage over the sea instead
Say you must think on it till the next tide
Before witnesses

There is no market place here: the strand street is the market. Before an open shed a countryman has three bundles of hides on a hand-cart and wants them gone before the tide. He names a low price, and looks up the street as he names it.

A gravel street along the top of a beach, house-sides with open sheds of cloth and black jugs: a countryman with three bundles of hides on a hand-cart glancing over his shoulder, a Frisian master feeling a hide, two idle men and a broad red-faced reeve watching from a doorway where a balance hangs.
Three bundles, good winter hides, and I must be on the road before dark. Ten the bundle. Eight, if we need not trouble the reeve's men for it.
Where from? Up the river. My own beasts. Does a hide have to say whose it was?
King Ine's law, shipman. A trader buys before witnesses, or he swears at the altar that he is no thief's friend. Thirty-six shillings if he cannot. I only say it.
You set wine on my table. I shall stand by this one myself, and my standing costs you nothing. Count his hides aloud.
Hides were sold in my street with nobody looking on. Then a man came down the river asking after his hides. I told him what I had not seen.
Buy before the reeve's two men (30 d, and 2 d for their trouble)
Buy with the reeve himself standing by (30 d)
Buy quickly, with nobody looking on (24 d)
Say hides are no cargo for a wine boat
The tall Dane's bridge

Ships bound upstream lie below the timber bridge waiting for slack water, the river heaping against the piers with a noise like a mill. The men on the bridge are Danes, in the English king's pay since the spring. The tallest of them leans on the rail and looks down into your boat.

A timber bridge on many piers with brown water heaping against it, ships waiting below at anchor: armed Danes along the rail, and among them a very tall man in a blue cloak with a gold arm-ring, leaning on the rail and looking down into a small trading boat.
You wait for slack water like the rest. Good. My men hold this bridge for the English king, and he feeds and clothes us for it. That is the bargain. I keep bargains.
They killed the archbishop with ox bones, drunk on southern wine. I offered all I had but my ship for his life. So now I stand on this side of the bridge.
Forty-five crews eat. The king's reeves send what they can, and it comes late and it comes mouldy. A man with corn in his boat need go no further than this bridge.
They say the Danish king comes himself this year. You have lain in his havens. How many keels, and how are they manned? I pay for a true count.
Twenty-one thousand pounds for my ships, and the English call me a robber for taking wages. I held their town when their own lords rode away.
Your count was true, near enough. I do not forget a man who can count.
Sell his quartermaster six sacks of wheat (48 d)
Tell him what lies in the Danish havens
Leave a penny at the bridge foot for the archbishop's soul
Wait for slack water with the rest, and say little
The king's new church

Upriver past the fields of the old wic lies an island of thorn and gravel with a small church, a landing and a fish weir. The east end of the island is all scaffolding now. A monk with keys at his girdle comes down to the landing, shouting to be heard over the masons.

A gravel island in a broad river with a small old church and a fish weir, and beyond it a great new stone church rising in scaffolding, masons on ladders, blocks on rollers: a monk with keys at his girdle on the landing stage, a salmon hung in the porch behind him.
A dozen of us sang here in a church you could cross in twelve steps. Now the king builds one longer than any in the kingdom, and the masons come from over the sea.
The roof wants lead, more than the hills send in a summer. Bring it by water to our own landing and the king's steward pays on the day. He is new to it.
A fisherman ferried a stranger over, the night before the first church was hallowed. The stranger was Saint Peter. So a salmon hangs in the porch each year, and the fishermen pay a tithe.
The king is not well. He wants the church hallowed while he can stand in it. The masons work by torchlight now.
You took the order for lead. The plumbers ask me every morning whether a Frisian keeps his day.
Take the order: six pigs of lead for the roof
Sell the lead you carry at the abbey's landing (2 pigs, 40 d)
Hear Mass in the old small church, and give a penny toward the new
Watch the masons a while
Carts for the city

The tide ends here. Beyond the last boat stands a heron, and beyond the heron an ox cart with solid wheels, its two beasts asleep on their feet. The carter is counting your casks from where he sits, and making it plain that he is in no hurry.

A low gravel bank on a narrow brown river among reeds, five boats lying stem to the bank with masts down: an ox cart with solid wheels and two sleepy oxen at the head of the hythe, a carter on the shaft counting on his fingers, a heron at the last boat.
The sea comes this far and no further. After this it is my oxen: up to the city gate with a load before the bell, and down again empty.
What sells for sixty on this bank sells for seventy at the cellarer's door. He will not come down for it. He sends me.
Christ Church says the cart is theirs. The abbey of the kings' graves says the oxen are. I belong to whichever is nearer when I am asked.
A man who was a priest calls himself king in the city this year. They shut the gate at dusk and look in every load. I say wine. They look anyway.
Your casks went up whole, and the cellarer paid on the cart tail. He asked whose they were. I said a Frisian who does not water.
Send two casks of wine up to the cellarer on his cart
Send four pairs of quernstones up to the bakers of the city
Ride up on the cart tail, and see the city
The two who watch

On the dry shingle above the weed line sacks of corn stand open, and a heap of grey salt lies on a hide. A woman of the island sits among the sacks with her sleeves rolled. Two men stand by her, and do nothing whatever but watch.

Dry shingle above a line of weed on a brown strait: open sacks of wheat, a heap of grey salt on a hide, baskets of oysters under wet weed, a farm wife with rolled sleeves sitting among them, two men standing idle beside her watching a Frisian master put his hand in a sack.
Wheat of the island, shipman, threshed this week. Put your hand in. You will not find better between here and the Thames, and on the Strand they give half as much again.
Those two? They watch. A bargain on this strand that nobody watched is a bargain somebody asks about. They cost a cup each, and I pay for one.
The nun says a book has it that this island feeds six hundred households. I feed seven people and a pig. The rest must be doing very well.
